title: Carbon farming

definition.text: A set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plant material.

facts.text: Its overall goal is a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked into soil and plants.
Converting forests, grasslands or savannas into cropland cuts the soil's organic carbon by about 30–40%.
Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using mulch or compost, adding biochar, and changing which crops are grown.
Mixing biochar into soil locks away roughly 50% of the carbon in the original biomass.
Carbon farming could offset as much as 20% of 2010 carbon dioxide emissions each year; by 2016 its variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares.
The stored carbon is not permanent: disturbing the soil or tilling intensively turns it back into a net source of greenhouse gases.
If incentives reward only stored carbon, it could encourage land clearing, monocultures and biodiversity loss.
Farmers who store carbon can sell carbon credits to companies that need offsets, as in Australia.

contested_note: Sources say the effect of more soil carbon on crop yield is unsettled, and critics doubt the practices can spread widely enough to matter.

definition.text: Growing bamboo plantations as a way to store carbon on farmland.

facts.text: A bamboo forest holds less total carbon than most mature forests but can match rubber plantations and orchards and exceed agroforests, palm oil plantations and grasslands.
Bamboo plantations take up carbon faster than mature forests, but only when new or actively managed.

title: 4 per 1000 initiative

definition.text: A France-led international effort to raise the carbon in farm and forest soils by 0.4% a year.

facts.text: It is the largest international effort to promote carbon farming.

notes: No page of its own; only the Carbon farming page mentions it. Keep only if it passes a curriculum test at selection.

title: Climate-smart agriculture

definition.text: A set of farming methods that try at once to adapt farming to climate change, raise yields for food security, and cut farm greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: The World Bank calls it practices and technologies that together boost productivity, build resilience and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
The FAO says it is not a new set of practices but an approach fitted to local contexts.
Examples include heat-tolerant crop varieties, mulching, boundary trees and suitable housing and spacing for cattle.
Carbon farming is one of its components.
Agriculture, forestry and land use produce 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Rainfed farming makes up 80% of global agriculture, so shifting rainfall threatens many poor farmers in Asia and Africa.
No accepted standard defines it, and critics call the label greenwashing for big businesses.

contested_note: Critics argue the label has no standard and can be used to greenwash.

definition.text: Designing climate-smart farming programmes to address the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

facts.text: Women farmers in developing countries face more climate risk because they have less access to land resources, money and advice.
They are often left out of decisions, which can limit their adoption of practices that help them adapt.

definition.text: A scoring tool that measures how resilient farming systems are to climate change.

facts.text: The global version benchmarks countries with nine indicators in three dimensions: productivity and resource efficiency, environmental sustainability and climate impact, and socio-economic resilience.
It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience.
A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare the country's agro-climatic zones.

definition.text: The heat-trapping gases released by farming, both directly from crops and livestock and indirectly from clearing land for farms.

facts.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of agriculture's direct emissions.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer contributes around 5% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.
Livestock production alone accounts for almost 60% of food-system greenhouse gas emissions.
Ruminants such as cows and sheep give off methane made by microbes in their guts.

title: Landscape-scale conservation

definition.text: An approach that manages a whole landscape to balance nature conservation against farming, forestry and other economic uses of the same land.

facts.text: It is an alternative to protecting single sites.
Its backers argue that poverty, food security, climate change, water scarcity and biodiversity loss are linked, so they need coordinated action across a landscape.
A river basin, for example, supplies water, timber, crops and habitat, and each use affects the others.
Rather than serving a single land use, it tries to meet the interests of many different stakeholders.
The IUCN applied it in 27 landscapes in 23 countries.
Often called the landscape approach, it was described by UNEP in 2015 as embodying ecosystem management.
Landscape approaches try to meet several Sustainable Development Goals at once, for example raising farm output, flood defence, biodiversity and carbon storage within one river catchment.
A review found five barriers, including confusing terminology, long delays before action, and sectors working in silos.

notes: Also covers the syllabus phrase concept 'Landscape approach' (phrase-working-lands), which the sources use as a synonym; no separate entry drafted.

definition.text: A way of managing a landscape sustainably by bringing together stakeholders who want different things from the land.

facts.text: Sara Scherr coined the term in 2012 for planning whole regions rather than single farms or plots.
By 2016 it had five steps: stakeholders meet, share information, plan together, carry out the plan, and monitor and adapt.
It seeks synergies among conservation, farm production and rural livelihoods.

title: Sustainable agriculture

definition.text: Farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively.

facts.text: Agriculture has a huge environmental footprint; food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions.
It aims to produce crops or livestock without damaging soil, water, biodiversity, or the people on and near the farm.
Its elements can include permaculture, agroforestry, mixed farming, multiple cropping and crop rotation.
In 1977 the USDA defined it as practices that, over the long term, meet food needs, improve the environment, use resources efficiently, keep farms viable and improve farmers' quality of life.
Environmental costs left out of a farmer's ordinary accounts are called externalities.
Investment in it is said to be four times more cost-effective than direct food aid, yet gets only three percent of humanitarian funds.
Many certification systems exist, including organic certification, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade.
People disagree on its definition: an ecocentric view favours low growth and organic methods, a technocentric view relies on technology and modified industry.

contested_note: Sources describe a debate over how to define sustainability in agriculture, between ecocentric and technocentric views.

definition.text: Farming methods that raise production while also improving environmental outcomes, without clearing more land.

facts.text: It differs from earlier intensification by putting weight on broader environmental results.
By 2018 an estimated 163 million farms in 100 nations used it, on 453 million ha, equal to 29% of farms worldwide.
Whether ecosystem services can replace non-renewable inputs while keeping yields high has been much debated.
In east Asian rice fields, nectar plants that support pest predators cut insecticide need by 70% with a 5% yield gain.

definition.text: A strategy that keeps farmland and nature strictly apart, farming some land intensively for high yields so that other land can stay wild.

facts.text: It has been the dominant strategy in developed countries for over 150 years.
Reviews find it generally favoured for conserving tropical forest biodiversity, in 67% of relevant studies.

definition.text: A strategy, also called wildlife-friendly agriculture, that makes room for biodiversity inside farmed areas by farming less intensively.

facts.text: Agroforestry and mixed crop-livestock systems are examples.
Reviews more often find it better for food security and livelihoods, in 58% of studies.

title: Land sparing versus land sharing

definition.text: The long scientific argument over whether nature is better protected by separating farms from wild land or by mixing them.

facts.text: The debate has run for over a decade without a clear consensus.
Sparing tends to win for tropical forest biodiversity, sharing for food security and livelihoods.
A third option, land blending, has been proposed because each strategy's success depends on the landscape.

contested_note: Scientists have debated the two strategies for over a decade with no clear consensus.

definition.text: An in-between strategy that mixes land sparing and land sharing to suit each landscape.

facts.text: It only recently emerged as a credible alternative; research suggests it can reconcile conservation and farming while building resilience.

definition.text: Farming focused on the environmental side of sustainable agriculture, using methods that rebuild ecosystem services.

facts.text: It aims to prevent erosion, improve water infiltration, store carbon as humus and raise biodiversity.
Techniques include no-till farming, multispecies cover crops, strip cropping, terraces and shelter belts.
Crop genetic diversity lowers the risks of monocultures, which can be vulnerable to a changing climate.

title: Multifunctional agriculture
article: Sustainable agriculture#Different viewpoints about the definition

definition.text: The view that farming does more than produce food and fibre, also managing renewable resources, conserving landscapes and supporting biodiversity.

facts.text: It is a farm-centred lens that treats these other functions as outputs of farming.
The rival ecosystem-services lens instead starts from benefits nature gives people, such as pollination, soil formation and nutrient cycling.

definition.text: A farming system, defined by the FAO, that protects farmland from loss and restores degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and a variety of crops.

facts.text: Its first principle, minimal soil disturbance such as no-till, keeps minerals in the soil and prevents erosion and water loss.
Its second principle, a permanent organic cover of mulch, shields the soil from rain and wind and builds organic matter.
Its third principle is diverse crop rotation, which breaks pest and weed cycles and improves water infiltration.
Farmers can save 30% to 40% of time and labour by not tilling.
Benefits come slowly: building organic matter takes years, and early years can bring financial losses.
Barriers include the high cost of special planting equipment and competition with livestock for crop residues.

title: Agri-environment schemes

definition.text: Programmes, compulsory for EU member states, that pay farmers to adopt environmentally friendlier methods to make up for the cost of changing.

facts.text: Farmers join voluntarily and commit for at least five years.
In 2009 they covered 38.5 million hectares, 20.9% of farmland in the then 27 EU states.
In 2012 the European Commission spent €3.23 billion on them, far more than the €39.6 million spent managing Natura 2000 sites.
Their aim shifted from protecting threatened habitats, to keeping wildlife on farmland, to improving services such as pollination.
A 2015 review found schemes that take land out of production did better at boosting species than in-production schemes.

conflicts.text: Agri-environment schemes became compulsory for every Member State under the Agenda 2000 (1999) reform.
conflicts.note: Conservation agriculture dates compulsory schemes to 1992 (b7bc0cacc0b0); Common Agricultural Policy places it in the Agenda 2000 (1999) reforms.

notes: No article of its own; mentioned on Conservation agriculture and Common Agricultural Policy.

title: Results-based agri-environment schemes

definition.text: Schemes that pay farmers for a measured environmental result, such as breeding birds or plant species counted, rather than for following set practices.

facts.text: Pure schemes pay only for outcomes; hybrid schemes also require some management actions.
They tend to raise farmer autonomy and tie payment clearly to conservation results.

notes: Described only in Conservation agriculture § Future development.

title: Agroecology

definition.text: The study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming systems, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment.

facts.text: The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement.
It is multidisciplinary, drawing on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history.
It studies agroecosystem properties such as productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability, at scales from a gene to the globe.
Unlike natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces governing agroecosystems.
Biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food are its three certified varieties; organics is practised in 188 countries.
Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue food sovereignty.
Researchers heatedly debate which model of agriculture or agroecology policy should support.

contested_note: Researchers debate which model of agriculture, including agroecology, policy should support.

definition.text: A way of managing land that grows trees together with crops or pasture on the same ground.

facts.text: It can yield timber, fruit, nuts, mushrooms, medicinal plants, animals and other products.
It is managed to make the most of helpful interactions between plants and animals, using the forest as a model, and is described as applied agroecology.
Benefits include higher farm productivity and profits, less soil erosion, wildlife habitat, more biodiversity and carbon sequestration, provided the farm is well managed.
Growing varied products such as fuelwood and medicinal plants makes farm income more secure.
Trees store carbon in soil and wood and can recapture some carbon lost when forests were cut.
It is most common on tropical smallholdings, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, and has spread to the US and Europe.
A survey of over 700 East African households found at least 50% had begun planting trees to adapt to climate change.
The term was coined in 1973 by forester John Bene, but the practice is millennia old.

definition.text: Growing strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges.

facts.text: Pruned tree leaves are spread over the crop to supply nutrients.
The hedges act as windbreaks, reduce erosion and suppress weeds with mulch and shade.

definition.text: Crops deliberately grown in the shade beneath a canopy of trees.

facts.text: Shade-grown coffee is a well-known example; shading cuts weeding costs and improves coffee quality.

definition.text: An organic agroforestry system, developed by Ernst Götsch in Brazil, that copies natural forest succession to build productive food forests.

facts.text: It relies on dense mixed planting of perennial and annual crops and on cutting fast-growing pioneer plants to build up nutrients.
Documented benefits include better water penetration, higher productivity on poor land and moderated soil temperature.

definition.text: Rows of trees or shrubs planted to slow the wind over and around crops.

facts.text: They raise yields by reducing crop drying and stopping plants from being blown over.
The USDA lists windbreaks as one of five temperate agroforestry practices.

definition.text: Growing high-value specialty crops under a forest canopy that is managed to give the right shade and habitat.

facts.text: It ranges from planting crops under timber trees to adjusting existing stands so their plants sell better.
In 1929 J. Russell Smith's book Tree Crops argued tree crops could replace cereals in animal feed and protect the environment.

definition.text: A low-maintenance way of producing food modelled on woodland, with layers of fruit and nut trees, shrubs, herbs, vines and perennial vegetables.

facts.text: Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest form of land use and remain common in the tropics as home gardens.
They are a significant source of income and food security for local people.
Robert Hart coined the term in the 1980s and adapted it to the UK's temperate climate.

definition.text: Applying agroforestry in towns, combining trees, shrubs and crops in gardens, parks and streets.

facts.text: Agroforestry on rooftop gardens can cut energy demand for cooling by up to 20%.
Because urban land is valuable, the opportunity cost of other land uses is a major constraint.

definition.text: A plant grown to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

facts.text: Cover crops help manage erosion, soil fertility, water, weeds, pests, diseases and wildlife on a farm.
They are often grown only to prevent erosion: roots anchor soil and the canopy slows raindrops and runoff.
A meta-analysis of 102 field studies found they raised topsoil organic carbon by about 10% and nitrogen by about 20%.
They reduce water pollution and take carbon dioxide out of the air.
Thick stands smother weeds, and some suppress weeds chemically through allelopathy.
In one study songbird densities were 7–20 times higher in cotton fields with a clover cover crop.
Effects on the next crop's water and yield vary, especially in semi-arid regions, and long-term profitability is uncertain.

definition.text: A cover crop grown to raise soil fertility, usually ploughed in before it matures.

facts.text: Green manures are commonly legumes, which are high in nitrogen and can supply what a crop needs.
This replaces nitrogen that conventional farms apply as chemical fertilizer.

definition.text: A crop grown to lure pests away from the valuable crop.

facts.text: Once pests gather, the small trap area can be treated or the pests physically removed.
Mustard and radish trap nematodes, cutting their populations by 70–99%.

title: Regenerative agriculture

definition.text: An approach to farming that aims to restore rather than just sustain, rebuilding topsoil, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

facts.text: It is not one practice but a combination of sustainable agriculture techniques, such as recycling farm waste and adding compost.
The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s.
A 2020 review of 229 articles and 25 websites found no legal or broadly accepted definition; some definitions name practices, others outcomes.
Its four most consistent principles are improving soil health, optimising resource use, easing climate change and improving water quality and availability.
An estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost since tillage-based farming began.

A 2023 review found reduced tillage, cover crops, crop–livestock integration and agroforestry can improve soil carbon or yields in some conditions, but evidence on benefits and profitability is limited.
Some scientists call proponents' climate claims exaggerated and unsupported.

contested_note: Scientists dispute claims that regenerative practices, especially grazing, can store enough carbon to counter climate change.

title: Holistic planned grazing

definition.text: Moving livestock herds constantly between fields to imitate how wild herds graze.

facts.text: Supporters say trampling restores soil, stimulates regrowth and raises soil carbon and water infiltration.
A meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it did no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass.
Allan Savory claimed in a TED talk that it could bring carbon dioxide back to pre-industrial levels in 40 years; critics reject this.

contested_note: Evidence on its carbon benefits is mixed, and critics reject the claim that it can reverse climate change.

definition.text: A strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from the effects of nearby land use.

facts.text: Buffers catch sediment, nutrients and pesticides in runoff before they reach the water.
They counter eutrophication downstream and stabilise banks against erosion.
They provide habitat and wildlife corridors in farming areas.
A nine-year University of Georgia study found buffers removed at least 60% of nitrogen and 65% of phosphorus from fertilizer runoff.
Buffers can raise land value and allow profitable crops such as black walnut and hazelnut.
Programmes such as the US Conservation Reserve Program pay farmers to make up for taking buffer land out of production.
A 2017 study found little ability to stop glyphosate leaching to streams.

definition.text: The usual three-zone layout of a riparian buffer, from stream-side trees to outer grass strips.

facts.text: The zone next to the water holds fast-growing native trees that shade the stream and stabilise the bank.
The middle zone of native shrubs gives wildlife habitat and absorbs what the outer zone misses.
The outer grass zone is the first defence, slowing runoff and absorbing contaminants.
A typical recommended width is 50 feet (15 m) on each side of the stream.

definition.text: A riparian buffer whose width follows local groundwater flow instead of a fixed distance.

facts.text: Groundwater enters streams at hotspots that matter disproportionately for temperature, acidity and nutrient retention.
Soil wetness maps from elevation models show where buffers should be wider.
Designing by hydrology rather than fixed width can save money in forestry.

definition.text: Combining trees, forage plants and grazing livestock on the same land so each benefits the others.

facts.text: It is a form of agroforestry that uses managed grazing.
Selling tree crops, forage and livestock together can raise productivity and long-term income.
Partial tree cover moderates temperature: one study found near-ground air up to 7% cooler than in open pasture.
Carbon uptake is lowest in open pastures, intermediate in silvopastures and highest in forests.
It needs heavy upfront investment and typically takes 3–6 years to give returns.
Barriers include policy hurdles, land tenure, lack of knowledge, economic constraints and cultural change.
If done correctly it can count as a nature-based solution to climate change.

definition.text: A traditional European system in which open woodland gave grazing animals shelter and forage while also yielding timber and fuel.

facts.text: It is one of the oldest land-use practices in human history.
Since Roman times, pigs have been turned into beech and oak woods to eat acorns and beech mast.

definition.text: An economic approach that aims to renew capital assets, treating the Earth as the original capital asset, instead of using them up.

facts.text: In standard theory an asset can be regenerated or consumed until it no longer yields goods or services.
Supporters say ignoring nature's value has caused uneconomic growth, Herman Daly's term, which they see as its opposite.
It has four components: circulation, organisational structure, relationships and values, and collective learning.
Unlike ecological economics, which sets limits on the economy, it focuses on the reproduction of life in nature.

definition.text: Investing that builds on sustainable finance to support ecological health, social well-being and economic resilience.

facts.text: It often, but not only, uses decentralized finance.

definition.text: Contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming.

facts.text: It comes from single discharge points and, more often, from diffuse non-point sources across the landscape, as well as air pollution.
Farm pollutants include sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts, reaching lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater.
Runoff concentrated in large water bodies causes dead zones downstream.
Poor management, such as overgrazing, ploughing and badly timed pesticide use, drives much of it.
Animal agriculture has an outsized impact on pollutants entering the environment.
Agricultural economists design incentives to control such externalities, for example water pollution from farming.

definition.text: The loss of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized fields into water and air, where they cause pollution.

facts.text: Fertilizers vastly raised yields: at 1900 yield levels, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land.
Nitrate dissolves easily, so it runs off into surface water and leaches into groundwater.
Nitrate above 10 mg/L in groundwater can cause blue baby syndrome in infants.
Phosphorus is the largest contributor to eutrophication, especially in fresh water.
Fertilization also releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that harms stratospheric ozone.

definition.text: The tendency of some pesticides to stay in the environment for many years after use.

facts.text: Without pest control, crop losses before harvest would typically reach 40 percent.
2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years; DDT and dieldrin are also long-lived.

title: Agricultural plastic pollution
article: Agricultural pollution#From equipment and agricultural plastics

definition.text: Plastic from greenhouse sheeting, storage bags, silage wrap and mulch film that ends up in farmed land.

facts.text: A 2021 FAO study estimated farming produces 10 million tons of plastic waste a year.
Very little agricultural plastic is collected worldwide.

title: Livestock greenhouse gas estimates
article: Agricultural pollution#Greenhouse gases from fecal waste

definition.text: The dispute over how large a share of human greenhouse gas emissions comes from livestock.

facts.text: The FAO estimated 18% of human greenhouse gases come directly or indirectly from livestock, more than transport.
Critics say the comparison is unfair because the FAO used a full life-cycle assessment for livestock but not for transport.
Others claim livestock could cause up to 51% of emissions.

contested_note: Estimates of livestock's share of emissions range from 18% to up to 51%, and the FAO method has been called a misrepresentation.

conflicts.text: The global livestock industry could be responsible for up to 51% of greenhouse gases.
conflicts.note: Contrasts with the FAO estimate of 18% (c72927210c59); the two rest on different accounting choices.

title: Biological pest control risks

definition.text: The debate over releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to control farm pests in place of pesticides.

facts.text: Biocontrol can cut pollution from pesticide use.
Once released, an agent may be impossible to recall and may spread into the wild or switch to native hosts.

contested_note: The merits of introducing non-native biocontrol agents are widely debated.

definition.text: Handling and treating animal waste to limit air, soil and water pollution.

facts.text: The EPA suggests one dairy farm with 2,500 cows makes as much waste as a city of around 411,000 people.
Treatment reduces the manure to transport, nutrients to spread and pathogens.
Anaerobic digestion breaks down liquid manure without air, producing fertilizer liquid and methane that can be burned for heat and power.

definition.text: The variety of living things found on farmland.

facts.text: Biodiversity on farms falls as varied landscapes are lost and native plants are replaced by crops.
The FAO estimates more than 40% of Earth's land surface is used for agriculture, making habitat loss the main driver of biodiversity loss.
Fallow land, grass margins and scrub strips between fields add habitat variety and so raise farm biodiversity.
Smaller fields have been linked to greater species richness.
In Asian rice, flowering strips beside fields cut insecticide spraying by 70% and raised yields by 5%, an economic advantage of 7.5%.
Low crop diversity can increase pests and pesticide resistance, causing ecological and economic losses.

definition.text: The variety of habitats and features across a farmed landscape, which supports a variety of species.

facts.text: Butterfly abundance has been found to increase with heterogeneity.
The Green Revolution, since 1966, spread a few crops such as wheat, rice and maize, reducing heterogeneity and local crop diversity.

definition.text: Growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons.

facts.text: It stops crops drawing on one set of nutrients and reduces pests, weeds and resistance.
Growing the same crop year after year, monocropping, drains particular nutrients and breeds specialised pests.
Rotating nitrogen-fixing legumes such as clover with nitrogen-hungry crops supplies nitrogen to later crops.
Rotations, especially diverse long ones, greatly increase soil organic carbon.
Changing crops interrupts pest life cycles and habitat.
Different crops spread the farmer's risk from bad weather.
In the Green Revolution, developed countries largely replaced rotation with chemical fertilizers.
US organic certification requires a crop rotation.

definition.text: A medieval European rotation dividing land into autumn crops, spring crops and a fallow field, rotated each year.

facts.text: Farmers in Europe moved to it from the two-field system between the 9th and 11th centuries, and it lasted until the 20th century.
Two thirds of the land was planted instead of half, and the legume crops improved people's nutrition.

definition.text: An 18th-century rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover that let livestock be kept all year.

facts.text: Charles Townshend popularised it, and it became a key development of the British Agricultural Revolution.

definition.text: The yield gain that rotated crops show compared with crops grown alone year after year.

facts.text: It arises mainly from relieving the problems of monoculture: better nutrition, less pest and weed stress and better soil structure.

definition.text: A line of shrubs, sometimes with trees, planted and trained as a barrier or boundary; old field-boundary hedges are called hedgerows.

facts.text: Hedges often act as windbreaks that improve conditions for crops.
The first hedges enclosed cereal fields in the Neolithic, 4000–6000 years ago.
They help prevent soil loss, reduce pollution, regulate water and reduce flooding.
One study found 100% of northwest European farms have hedges, providing 43% of the wildlife habitat there.
Removing hedges makes bigger, cheaper-to-farm fields with more yield and profit, but weakens soil and causes erosion.
UK hedge removal was subsidised after World War II, and over half of UK hedgerows have vanished since the 1950s.
The UK government now increasingly compensates farmers for maintaining them.

definition.text: A rule of thumb that estimates a hedge's age as the number of woody species in a thirty-yard stretch times 110 years.

facts.text: Max Hooper published it in 1974; it can be off by a couple of centuries and fails for hedges over a thousand years old.

definition.text: Restoring a hedge by cutting most of the way through each stem near the base, bending it over and weaving it between stakes.

facts.text: It encourages new growth from the base and was originally done to keep hedges stock-proof.

definition.text: A pest control approach that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to control pests economically while relying less on pesticides.

facts.text: The FAO describes it as combining biological, chemical, physical and cultural methods to grow healthy crops with minimal pesticide use.
It aims at control, not eradication, since wiping out a pest is often impossible, costly and unsafe.
Prevention comes first: resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping.
It reduces risks such as pest resurgence, pesticide resistance and residues on food.
Alternating between classes of control helps stop pests becoming resistant.
It runs as six repeated steps: sample, identify, learn the pest's biology, set an action threshold, choose tactics, evaluate.
In 1986 Indonesia banned 57 pesticides and stopped subsidising them.

definition.text: The pest population at which the crop damage would cost more than treating the pest.

facts.text: The economic threshold is the lower population at which action must be taken to stop pests reaching the economic injury level.
IPM sets these action thresholds from estimated economic damage and treats only when they are exceeded.
Thresholds depend on the pest and the site.
Letting a pest survive at a tolerable level reduces selection pressure for resistance.

definition.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

facts.text: Its main goal is a larger total yield by using resources a single crop would leave unused.
Crops are paired to avoid competing, such as deep-rooted with shallow-rooted, or tall with shade-tolerant.
In low-input systems it can give higher yields for the same input, or steadier yields with less.
A companion crop can support plants prone to falling over, or supply nutrients.
Results vary: a 2008 review found predators rose in only 53% of studies and yields in only 32%.
Crop rotation differs because its crops grow in separate seasons.

definition.text: Sowing a second crop while the first is still growing, so the first is harvested to make room for the second.

facts.text: Related temporal intercropping pairs a fast-growing crop with a slow one, harvesting the fast crop first, and can out-yield either alone.

definition.text: Pest control that pairs an attractive trap crop pulling pests in with a repellent crop pushing them away from the main crop.

facts.text: In a 2006 review of 100 trap crops, only 10 succeeded commercially, all with added measures to stop insects returning to the main crop.

definition.text: Growing crops between rows of nitrogen-fixing Inga trees, whose pruned leaves form a thick mulch.

facts.text: It lets land be farmed repeatedly, offering an alternative to destructive slash-and-burn cultivation.
Mike Hands developed and trialled it in Costa Rica in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

title: No-till farming

definition.text: Growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

facts.text: It reduces erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils, and can improve water infiltration, organic matter and nutrient cycling.
Worldwide area grew from about 45 million ha in 1999 to 111 million ha in 2009.
In Argentina it cut erosion losses by 80% and costs by more than 50%; in Paraguay net farm incomes rose 77%.
Fewer machinery passes lower fuel and labour costs.
Without tillage to remove weeds, farmers commonly use herbicides such as glyphosate, increasing herbicide use.
Nitrogen tied up in residue can mean higher fertilizer rates, and cold, wet spring soil can delay planting.
Whether it increases soil carbon is debated; some studies suspect flawed testing or losses deeper in the soil.
England's DEFRA pays farmers £73 per hectare to convert.

contested_note: Sources debate whether the extra soil carbon reported under no-till is real or an artefact of testing methods.

definition.text: A group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled.

facts.text: No-till and strip tillage are both forms of it, but no-till is not the same thing.
Tillage, mechanically stirring the soil, has been used since at least 3000 B.C.
By 2014 more than 75% of Canadian Prairie cropland had adopted it.

title: Organic farming

definition.text: A farming system that relies on natural inputs such as compost, manure and green manure and on methods like crop rotation, and largely bans synthetic pesticides and fertilizers.

facts.text: Genetically modified organisms, sewage sludge, growth hormones and routine antibiotics in livestock are prohibited.
It began early in the 20th century as a reaction to fast-changing farming.
By 2022 it was practised in 188 countries on about 96,000,000 hectares by 4.5 million farmers.
The organic market reached $150 billion worldwide in 2022.
On average 30% more species live on organic farms, though this ignores extra land needed for lower yields.
A 2012 meta-analysis found organic farming needs 84% more land for the same harvest.
Emissions per area of land are lower, but per unit of food nitrogen leaching and related pollution are higher.
There is not enough evidence that organic food is safer or healthier than conventional food.

contested_note: Sources disagree on its environmental record: lower impact per hectare but often higher impact per unit of food because yields are lower.

definition.text: Rules, voluntary or set by law, that define how organic food must be produced and allow it to be labelled organic.

facts.text: Private groups certified organic producers in the 1970s; legislated standards spread from the 1991 EU regulation.
By 2007 over 60 countries regulated organic farming.
Agencies usually accredit certification groups rather than individual farms.

definition.text: The higher price organic food fetches over conventional food, which is key to whether organic farming pays.

facts.text: With premiums, US organic farming was 2.7 to 3.8 times more profitable; globally 22–35% more profitable.
In 2013 premiums were 100% for organic vegetables and 57% for organic fruit.
Globally, premiums of only 5-7% were needed to break even with conventional farming.
Premiums have narrowed, weakening the incentive to convert; without them profitability is mixed.

title: Organic yield gap

definition.text: The difference between organic and conventional crop yields and whether organic farming could feed the world.

facts.text: A 2012 meta-analysis found organic productivity on average 25% lower.
The gap depends on crop and site: about 5% for rain-fed legumes and perennials, about 13% under best organic practice.
In 2007 the FAO said organic farming could not feed the current population.

contested_note: Estimates of the yield gap vary widely with crop, site and study.

conflicts.text: A 2011 meta-analysis of 362 datasets found organic yields were on average 80% of conventional yields.
conflicts.note: Implies a 20% average gap, against the 25% lower productivity of the 2012 meta-analysis (f894364f9d07).

title: Permaculture

definition.text: An approach to designing land use and settlements that copies the arrangements found in thriving natural ecosystems.

facts.text: It rests on design principles drawn from whole-systems thinking, applied to farming, town planning, rewilding and community resilience.
Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term in 1978, in opposition to industrial farming methods.
Earlier ideas of permanent agriculture, such as F. H. King's 1911 book and J. Russell Smith's Tree Crops of 1929, inspired it.
Holmgren set out twelve design principles, such as observe and interact, catch and store energy, and obtain a yield.
It favours perennial crops that need no yearly tilling and planting.
Critics say it is loosely defined and largely isolated from scientific literature.

contested_note: Critics argue permaculture lacks a clear definition and a scientific basis.

definition.text: The three core ethics of permaculture: care of the Earth, care of people, and setting limits to consumption and sharing the surplus.

facts.text: Mollison formulated them in 1988; Holmgren restated the third in 2002 as setting limits to consumption and reproduction and redistributing surplus.

definition.text: A layout that places parts of a design by how often people use them, numbered 0 to 5 outward from the house.

facts.text: Elements tended or harvested often go close to the house in zones 1 and 2; those used less are farther out.

definition.text: A mutually beneficial group of species that each provide different services within a larger ecosystem.

facts.text: Guild plants may supply food, draw up deep nutrients, fix nitrogen, attract helpful insects or repel pests.

definition.text: Burying wood in mounds or beds so that it soaks up water and keeps the soil moist.

facts.text: Enough buried wood can hold rainy-season water to carry crops through the dry season.

definition.text: Layering materials such as leaves, cardboard and wood chips over soil to imitate a forest floor.

facts.text: Mulch absorbs rain, cuts evaporation, adds organic matter, suppresses weeds and reduces erosion.
It is also used in regenerative agriculture to smother weeds and feed the soil.

definition.text: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use before it runs off or soaks into the ground.

facts.text: It supplies drinking water, livestock water and irrigation, and roof collection can significantly add to drinking water supply.

title: Rotational grazing

definition.text: Moving livestock between sections of pasture, called paddocks, so that the rest of the pasture can recover.

facts.text: It usually yields less than intensive livestock operations but needs fewer inputs, so net income per animal can be higher.
Each cow produces less, but more cows can graze each acre, giving more output per acre at less cost.
Pastures under some rotational systems erode less, and it may reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Manure returns most nutrients to the pasture, and swards with over 40% legumes need no commercial nitrogen.
Grazing animals on young legume-rich pasture risks bloat, which can be fatal.
In 87% of experiments, plant production was equal or greater under continuous grazing.
Virtual fencing with GPS collars can automate rotations.

contested_note: Scientists dispute whether rotational grazing beats continuous grazing for ecological goals; results depend on the management model.

definition.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion and the loss of fertility from overuse, acidification, salinization or contamination.

facts.text: Deforestation typically causes large-scale erosion, nutrient loss and sometimes desertification.
Techniques include crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage and windbreaks.
Farmers have practised it for millennia.
The EU's Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover crops, plant residues and grass margins.
Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, including changing how land is valued.
Each one percent increase in soil organic matter lets soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre.
Taxing pesticides at different rates is one option studied for cutting their use.

definition.text: Ploughing furrows along a slope's contour lines so they stay level, which slows runoff.

facts.text: It can raise crop yields by 10 to 50 percent, partly by keeping soil in place.
The ancient Phoenicians used it on slopes of two to ten percent.

definition.text: Cutting a hillside into a series of nearly level steps for growing crops.

facts.text: Terraces slow the rapid runoff of irrigation water and are more common on small farms.

definition.text: An extension of contour farming that shapes contour lines around the whole watershed.

facts.text: It is used in regenerative farms alongside diverse livestock and crop production.

definition.text: Preventing and reducing the build-up of salt in soil, which mainly comes from irrigating with salty water.

facts.text: Salt breaks down soil structure and causes infertility; salinity affects about one third of the earth's arable land.
After the 1970 Aswan Dam, a raised water table salinised soils in Egypt.
Salt-tolerant plants such as saltbush can lower water tables and slow surface salt build-up.

title: Soil health

definition.text: The state of a soil that performs the full range of ecosystem functions suited to its environment.

facts.text: It arises from good interactions among a soil's living and non-living parts, such as microbes, plants and animals.
It covers sustaining productivity, biodiversity, water and air quality, and human health.
The term has largely replaced soil quality, which judged soil only for one purpose such as growing maize.
It depends on soil biodiversity and improves when soil is kept covered and given carbon-rich amendments.
Some microbiologists believe 80% of soil nutrient functions are controlled by microbes.
US soils have lost up to 75% of their carbon over 40 years, though how much is debated.
A soil can be healthy for ecosystems without directly serving crop production, so terms and measures are debated.

contested_note: Scientists debate how to define and measure soil health, since ecological and agronomic goals can conflict.

definition.text: Measuring a soil's physical, chemical and biological condition against benchmarks of healthy function.

facts.text: Benchmarks include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium.
Many labs resist new biological tests because fertility testing rests on crop-response models with no equivalent for soil health.
